197 FERC ¶ 61,019
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ACCEPTING TARIFF REVISIONS IN PART 
AND REJECTING TARIFF REVISIONS IN PART

(Issued October 9, 2026)

On August 13, 2026, pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA), PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) submitted proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) and Reliability Assurance Agreement (RAA) (collectively, Tariff) to establish:  (1) a definition of Large Load; (2) a Large Load Registry; (3) a new Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS); (4) a requirement for Load Serving Entities (LSE) serving New Large Load to designate new capacity resources in an amount at least equal to the New Large Load’s peak load to avoid the New Large Load being subject to IRAS; (5) rules for Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) arrangements; and (6) rules to exclude Eligible New Large Load from the Variable Resource Requirement (VRR) curve beginning with Delivery Year 2029/2030.  
In this order, we accept PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions to establish a definition of Large Load and a Large Load Registry, effective October 12, 2026, as requested, and require PJM to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of issuance of this order.  We reject PJM’s remaining proposed Tariff revisions, as discussed below.
Filing Overview
PJM states that, beginning in the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, it will be short of sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement, particularly due to data center load growth and the pace of data center interconnection.  PJM’s proposal to address this challenge includes several elements:  (1) a definition of Large Load; (2) a Large Load Registry, which is a database of information pertaining to Large Loads that PJM proposes to establish and maintain; (3) IRAS, which PJM states will involve curtailments during periods when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand in real-time operations; (4) a requirement for LSEs serving New Large Load to designate new capacity resources in an amount at least equal to the New Large Load’s peak load; (5) rules for BYONC arrangements; and (6) rules to exclude Eligible New Large Load from the VRR curve beginning with Delivery Year 2029/2030.  PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions, as described further below, would implicate and assign responsibilities to several entities in PJM, including the Electric Distributor, the LSE, and the Transmission Owner.
PJM states that each element of the filing is severable, although some elements build upon each other.  PJM explains that, to facilitate Commission approval and smoothly implement its IRAS framework on June 1, 2027, PJM consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever the proposed Tariff language, as needed and permitted under the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, “where such modification is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives.”  PJM requests that, if the Commission elects to modify or sever any portion of the proposal, it should expressly prescribe the revised rate or rule.  The majority of PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions are not intended to take effect until June 1, 2027, consistent with the start of the 2027/2028 Delivery Year.  However, PJM requests an effective date for its entire filing of October 12, 2026, which PJM argues is necessary so that it may modify the planning parameters for the VRR curve underlying the 2029/2030 Base Residual Auction (BRA) in time for the 2029/2030 BRA set to run in December 2026.  
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of PJM’s filing was published in the Federal Register, 91 Fed. Reg. 53407 (Aug. 18, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before September 3, 2026.  Notices of intervention and timely-filed motions to intervene were submitted by the entities listed in the Appendix of this order, which also lists the abbreviated names for each entity and identifies those entities that submitted comments and protests.  
On August 28, 2026, OPSI filed a motion requesting an extension of time to submit comments in response to PJM’s filing.  On August 31, 2026, Google submitted an answer in support of OPSI’s motion.  On September 1, 2026, EKPC and Pennsylvania Commission submitted answers in support of OPSI’s motion.  On September 2, 2026, the Commission issued a notice denying OPSI’s motion. 
On September 3, after the 5:00 p.m. deadline, OPSI and Voltus each filed          out-of-time comments, and Equinix filed an out-of-time protest.  On September 4, CyrusOne filed a motion to intervene out-of-time.  On September 8, 2026, the Virginia Commission filed out-of-time comments.  On September 11, 2026, CyrusOne filed     out-of-time comments.  On September 11, 2026, Governor Shapiro filed a motion to intervene out-of-time.  On September 15, 2026, IECA filed out-of-time comments. 
On September 16, 2026, Governor Shapiro filed a motion for leave to answer and an answer to certain comments and protests.  On September 18, 2026, Buckeye and NJBPU each filed motions for leave to answer and an answer to certain comments and protests.  On September 23, 2026, PJM filed a motion for leave to answer and an answer to certain comments and protests.  On September 25, 2026, AEP filed a motion for leave to answer and an answer to certain comments and PJM’s answer.  On September 28, 2026, Representative Pallone filed out-of-time comments; and CEBA and Vistra each filed motions for leave to answer and an answer to certain comments and answers.  On September 29, 2026, AEU, Constellation, and Voltus each filed motions for leave to answer and answer to certain answers.  On September 30, 2026, Google filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain comments, protests, and answers.  On      October 1, 2026, Data Center Coalition filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain comments, protests, and answers.  On October 2, 2026, FirstEnergy filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain comments, protests, and answers.  On     October 6, 2026, PPL filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain answers.  On October 7, 2026, EPKC and SMECO each filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain answers.  On October 8, 2026, PAG filed out-of-time comments.  On      October 9, 2026, IMM filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to certain answers.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,        18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.
Pursuant to Rule 214(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,     18 C.F.R. § 385.214(d), we grant CyrusOne and Governor Shapiro’s late-filed motions to intervene given their interest in the proceeding, the early stage of the proceeding, and the absence of undue prejudice or delay.  We also accept the out-of-time comments and protests submitted by CyrusOne, Equinix, IECA, OPSI, PAG, Representative Pallone, the Virginia Commission, and Voltus.
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by AEP, AEU, Buckeye, CEBA, Constellation, Data Center Coalition, EKPC, FirstEnergy, Google, Governor Shapiro, IMM, NJBPU, PJM, PPL, SMECO, Vistra, and Voltus because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
PJM’s proposal consists of several elements that, when combined, are intended to address the capacity shortfall that, absent the entrance of new capacity resources, will prevent PJM from satisfying the PJM Region Reliability Requirement starting in the 2027/2028 Delivery Year.  The first element of PJM’s proposal is to establish definitions of Large Load and New Large Load.  The latter is designed to capture the Delivery Year when PJM’s capacity shortfall, which PJM contends is the result of data center load growth, first emerges.  Next, PJM proposes to develop a Large Load Registry to foster transparency regarding Large Load additions.  With that foundation, PJM proposes to adopt the IRAS framework, under which LSEs that seek to use Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) to serve New Large Loads must designate sufficient new capacity resources, referred to as BYONC, to serve the New Large Load.  If an LSE using NITS to serve New Large Load fails to designate sufficient capacity resources, such New Large Load will be “subject to load reduction requests” when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand in real-time operations.  In essence, the requirement that these New Large Loads must curtail under certain emergency conditions is designed to allow PJM to address its capacity shortfall.  
As outlined in greater detail below, we accept PJM’s proposal in part, effective October 12, 2026, as requested, reject PJM’s proposal in part, and direct PJM to submit a compliance filing within 30 days of the date of this order.  Specifically, we accept PJM’s proposal to establish a definition for Large Load and a Large Load Registry.  We find that those two elements of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Given PJM’s consent to sever or modify its proposal, we do so here.  We find that the elements of PJM’s proposal to establish a new definition of Large Load and a Large Load Registry are severable from the remainder of the filing and therefore may be accepted even though we reject the remainder of the proposal.
While we recognize the imminent capacity shortfall in PJM, we find that two key aspects of PJM’s proposal—IRAS and BYONC—are either outside of the Commission’s authority or have not been sufficiently demonstrated to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  We do not take this decision lightly.  But given the significant discrepancies between PJM’s transmittal letter description of its proposed IRAS framework and its proposed Tariff revisions, as well as the lack of justification for many aspects of IRAS and BYONC, we cannot find that these elements of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable.  We therefore reject these elements of the proposal.  However, we provide guidance on how PJM could modify its proposal should PJM seek to refile it.
Moreover, because the elements of PJM’s proposal other than the Large Load definition and Large Load Registry represent an integrated package that must be viewed as a whole, we reject the remainder of PJM’s proposal.  PJM, while consenting to severance and modification of the proposal, acknowledges that the RAA and OATT revisions are “designed to work in lockstep and provide complementary pieces.”  We find that the remaining elements of PJM’s proposal, such as the proposed rules for BYONC arrangements and the exclusion of Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR curve, are not simply complementary, but instead are inextricably linked.  For example, the new obligation for LSEs seeking to use NITS to serve New Large Load to bring new capacity to avoid curtailment under IRAS is foundational to both the IRAS and BYONC frameworks.  It also establishes the need for the rules for BYONC arrangements and facilitates excluding Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR curve.  As such, we conclude that, contrary to PJM’s statements in its transmittal, the only elements of its proposal that are severable are the proposed definition of Large Load and the proposed Large Load Registry, which can be implemented independent of the IRAS and BYONC frameworks.
Large Load Definition and Registry
Definition of Large Load  
PJM’s Proposal
PJM proposes to define Large Load as: 	
end-use customer(s) load that has a cumulative peak load of 50 [MW] or greater at a single electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection, where for configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points of interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them, all affiliated load facilities within a one-mile radius will be considered a single electrical site as further described in the PJM Manuals.  
Acknowledging that the Commission recently stated that PJM may establish its own definition of large load, PJM states that its definition differs from the Commission’s preliminary definition in several ways, and that these differences reflect the characteristics and realities of Large Loads in the PJM Region.  The differences include:  (1) setting a 50 MW cumulative peak threshold; (2) establishing a one-mile radius at a single electrical site for Large Loads interconnected at multiple points; (3) using the term “end-use customer(s) load” instead of “new, commercial or industrial customer;” (4) including co-located loads and loads with behind-the-meter generation; and (5) excluding a voltage threshold.  PJM states that it proposes to define a Large Load as located at a single electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection within a one-mile radius to avoid a scenario where, for example, a data center owner is not categorized as Large Load simply because the owner has elected to site a number of smaller data centers, each with peak loads below 50 MW, close together.  PJM states that the Commission has explicitly adopted a one-mile test in other situations to determine whether facilities are “at the same site” to be a Qualifying Facility.  
PJM states that Large Load is not limited to “new” load, and instead proposes a separate definition, “New Large Load,” to capture the temporal aspect of such load with greater specificity.  PJM proposes that New Large Load shall mean: 
end-use customer load that is either (a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.  However, to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years meet the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii),[] then New Large Load shall mean end-use customer load that is either (a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1 of the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1 of the first Delivery Year for which the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(b)(iii) are not met that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.
Pleadings
Protesters argue that PJM has not properly justified the 50 MW threshold for Large Loads.  EPSA, for example, asserts that PJM has articulated no valid reason why a new 49.9 MW load will not be subject to IRAS.  The IMM argues that the 50 MW cutoff will exclude a significant number of data centers.  On the other hand, some parties argue that the threshold should be higher or that PJM has not justified including types of load other than data centers in the definition of Large Load.  FirstEnergy argues that the definition of Large Load should be adjusted, either to raise the minimum MW threshold to 200 MW, or to limit the definition to new data centers, to avoid capturing small and medium-sized manufacturing facilities.  FirstEnergy acknowledges that similar energy infrastructure must be built regardless of the type of load, but that manufacturing should not be subject to IRAS because it generates investment and jobs, whereas data centers do not.  EKPC similarly argues that PJM’s justification for IRAS is based on data center load, and PJM has not justified the inclusion of industrial and manufacturing load, which does not present the same timing, concentration, or operational risks as data centers.  
Some protesters also assert that PJM’s distinction between new and existing Large Loads turns solely on an arbitrary date and has not been justified.  They argue that PJM has not explained why load that goes into service on May 31, 2027, should be treated differently from load that goes into service just one day later, on June 1, 2027.  Industrial Customers and IECA assert that only incremental expansions of load that are greater than 50 MW should be subject to IRAS and that PJM’s definitions of new and existing Large Load establish a baseline load value for existing Large Load customers based on historical usage and allow customers to demonstrate that growth is a normal fluctuation.  
Protesters argue that the definition of New Large Load fails to protect existing commercial arrangements or argue for grandfathering rules for pre-expansion load.  Protesters also seek clarity on how the proposed definition will apply to multi-year projects developed in phases, some of which are built prior to June 1, 2027 and some after.  Equinix and CyrusOne contend that PJM’s one-mile aggregation rule for Large Loads is unjust and unreasonable as applied to independently developed legacy data center facilities.  In addition, ODEC argues that PJM should clarify how affiliation will be determined for the purposes of the one-mile radius measurement.  
In its answer, PJM highlights the importance of timely Commission approval of the definition of Large Load.  In response to arguments that the 50 MW threshold is unsupported and should be changed, PJM asserts that the 50 MW threshold is in keeping with what was contemplated by the Commission and that no information presented renders PJM’s proposed threshold unjust and unreasonable.  Further, PJM contends that, since PJM has proposed that 50 MW is the appropriate threshold necessary for purposes of tracking Large Loads and ensuring PJM has visibility into them to ensure reliability, it would be contradictory to ignore any MW that may have existed as a Large Load before an additional 50 MW were added.
In response to parties’ arguments that PJM should differentiate between data center Large Loads and other types of Large Loads (e.g., manufacturing or industrial loads), PJM asserts that it is implementing the approach the Commission set forth in the PJM Large Load Show Cause Order—i.e., treating data center and computational, manufacturing, industrial, or other types of large loads the same.  PJM argues that the parties have shown no basis for deviating from the Commission’s approach.
In its answer, Data Center Coalition argues the PJM’s one-mile rule is not just and reasonable.  Data Center Coalition argues that the proposed one-mile rule would unfairly subject long-operating legacy facilities to IRAS and potential curtailment merely because an unrelated facility is later developed nearby, despite those legacy loads having already been accounted for through regional planning.  Data Center Coalition also argues that PJM’s undefined use of “affiliated” to aggregate facilities within a one-mile radius could improperly treat independent facilities as a single Large Load; therefore, Data Center Coalition asserts, the term’s criteria and application should be clearly specified in the Tariff rather than deferred to the PJM Manuals.  The IMM similarly argues that PJM has not provided clear, uniform criteria for applying the one-mile radius rule or defined “affiliated load facilities,” creating uncertainty about how co-located or connected data centers should be grouped.
FirstEnergy argues that PJM has not justified applying the Large Load definition to manufacturing or other industrial facilities because, unlike data centers, short-notice curtailment of manufacturing facilities may disrupt product and supply chains, strand inventory, damage equipment, and require costly cleaning and restart procedures. 
EKPC argues that PJM does not justify the 50 MW threshold and requests that the Commission should either require PJM to narrow the definitions or to establish objective criteria demonstrating that non-computational load presents the same IRAS-relevant risks.  The IMM argues that the 50 MW threshold would exclude a significant and growing share of data center load and that lowering the threshold would more effectively prevent gaming and reflect advances in prefabricated, scalable data center technology.
Determination
We find that PJM’s proposed definition of Large Load is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  First, we find that establishing the threshold to qualify as a Large Load at a cumulative peak of 50 MW strikes a just and reasonable balance between capturing the larger loads into which PJM needs visibility to ensure the reliability of its system and excluding smaller loads that do not raise the same reliability concerns in PJM.  We acknowledge protesters’ arguments that PJM has not explained why a new 49.9 MW load should not be subject to the same requirements as a new        50 MW load.  But any cutoff criterion would inevitably exclude loads sized just below the threshold, and that alone does not render the definition unjust or unreasonable.  
In addition, we disagree with protesters’ arguments that the definition of Large Load should be modified to exclude manufacturing facilities and include only data centers.  Protesters do not appear to argue that other types of large loads do not use energy at the same magnitude as data centers or do not have the same potential impacts on the transmission system.  Nor do protesters appear to argue that other types of large loads otherwise have different effects on resource adequacy that would justify excluding them from the definition of Large Load.  As such, we find reasonable PJM’s proposal to include all types of large loads in the Large Load definition.  
We acknowledge that commenters put forth alternate definitions of Large Load in the record.  However, having found PJM’s proposed definition of Large Load just and reasonable, as discussed above, we need not opine on these alternate definitions.  For filings made under FPA section 205, the Commission evaluates whether the proposal in the filing is just and reasonable, and not whether alternative proposals are more or less reasonable than the filing party’s proposal.
We also disagree with protesters’ arguments that defining a Large Load as a single electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection within a one-mile radius is unjust and unreasonable.  As PJM explains, the one-mile radius paired with the single electrical site requirement is necessary to ensure that loads that are physically located together and affiliated are considered as a single facility for the purposes of the Large Load definition.  We agree with PJM that this requirement will preclude a scenario where, for example, a data center load is not categorized as Large Load simply because the owner has elected to site a number of smaller data centers, each with peak loads below 50 MW, close together.  Regarding ODEC’s request for clarification for how affiliation will be determined for the purposes of measuring the one-mile radius, we note that “affiliate” is a defined term in the Tariff, and PJM explains that it intends to detail in the PJM Manuals the method of calculating the one-mile distance and for examining different configurations to determine whether they may constitute a single electrical site.  We agree with PJM that these are implementation details that are not necessary to include in the Tariff.
We find that PJM’s proposal to add a definition of New Large Load is fundamentally a part of PJM’s IRAS package, discussed below.  PJM explains that the term New Large Load is needed to describe the subset of Large Loads that PJM proposes may be subject to curtailment where the LSE does not designate capacity to offset the load.  Given that we are rejecting these aspects of PJM’s proposal, as discussed below, we also sever and reject the definition of New Large Load without prejudice.  While we do not reach the merits of the definition of New Large Load, we note that protesters argue that the definition of New Large Load does not protect existing commercial arrangements for incremental large load additions to existing Large Loads, and because we do not reach the merits of the definition of New Large Load, we do not address protesters’ remaining comments related to the definition of New Large Load.  Should PJM choose to refile a modified version of its proposed IRAS framework, we encourage PJM to address how its definition of New Large Load would be tailored to protect existing commercial arrangements.
Because we reject PJM’s proposed definition of New Large Load, we direct PJM to submit a compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of this order, with OATT and RAA revisions that include only the definition of Large Load and do not include the definition of or references to New Large Load.  
Large Load Registry
PJM’s Proposal
PJM proposes to require LSEs to submit information to PJM about the Large Loads they serve, which PJM will maintain in a Large Load Registry.  Specifically, PJM proposes revisions to Schedule 11 of the RAA to establish a registry of Large Loads in the PJM Region capturing existing Large Loads and New Large Loads that will interconnect in the future.  PJM explains the Large Load Registry will include information such as the Eligible Customer for the Large Load; a description of the Large Load; its location; the in-service date for each increment of load; any peak shaving adjustment value; the delivery point/point of interconnection; peak load quantity and ramp schedule; telemetry specifications; backup generation including fuel type and permitting limitations; contracts or service agreements between the Large Load and the LSE; points of contact at the applicable transmission owner, Electric Distributor, and LSE; and other details as necessary in accordance with the PJM Manuals.  PJM proposes to maintain the confidentiality of the information in the Large Load Registry consistent with PJM’s existing confidentiality obligations under Operating Agreement, section 18.17.
PJM states that the purpose of this registry is to:  (1) enable PJM to better forecast load growth, plan and manage the transmission system, and study and provide the anticipated new transmission services for co-located loads and Large Loads; and (2) make information available to Authorized Commissions, Transmission Owners, Electric Distributors, LSEs, the IMM, the Commission, and other entities pursuant to the Operating Agreement, subject to appropriate confidentiality and data protection safeguards.  PJM likewise notes that this information will be useful for states in monitoring adherence to Large Loads’ commitments to bringing capacity to offset demand and protect against higher prices for other customers, as well as implementing their own retail constructs.  PJM also proposes to aggregate data from the Large Load Registry and post it on the PJM website.  Additionally, PJM states that it will use the Large Load Registry to implement its proposed IRAS framework.
PJM proposes to require that the information used to develop and maintain the Large Load Registry be “submit[ted] or cause to be submitted” to PJM by LSEs.  In addition, PJM proposes to obtain information from Electric Distributors to coordinate with applicable Transmission Owners and Electric Distributors, as needed, to validate the information provided in the Large Load Registry or to consult with relevant Large Loads.  PJM states that the Commission has previously accepted proposals by PJM to require and obtain information from jurisdictional entities such as Electric Distributors and LSEs.  PJM argues that its authority to obtain “data and details concerning large load additions” finds support in the PJM Large Load Show Cause Order, which expressly required PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners to post and regularly update data and details concerning large load additions.  
Pleadings
Several parties support the creation of a Large Load Registry.  Google asserts that the Commission has the authority to accept only the Large Load Registry and should sever the remainder of the proposal.  According to Google, this approach would be consistent with PJM’s goals of improving resource adequacy in the region while ensuring that service to existing residential customers remains reliable.  Public Interest Organizations (PIO) argue that PJM’s proposal addresses some of the concerns related to large load interconnection, cost transparency, and reliability impacts laid out in the PJM Large Load Show Cause Order by proposing to establish a Large Load Registry.  Many state consumer advocates assert that they support the Large Load Registry, but argue that excluding state consumer advocates from the category of entities eligible to access confidential Large Load Registry information is not just and reasonable.  Some commenters suggest additional improvements to the database.
Protesters object to the responsibility for accuracy and any costs for compliance for the Large Load Registry falling on Transmission Owners and Electric Distributors.  Joint Consumer Advocates assert that, because the Large Load Registry is critical to the success of IRAS, it is unreasonable that, under PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry, New Large Loads apparently bear no affirmative, Tariff-expressed obligation either to submit data or to substantiate it.  SMECO similarly asserts that the proposed Large Load Registry’s data reporting mandate is deferred to future PJM Manual revisions, with no mechanism identified for Electric Distributors to recover the costs of compliance.  SMECO requests that the Commission require PJM to file Manual provisions for review before the Large Load Registry becomes effective, clarify the scope of Electric Distributor liability for information sourced from LSEs or Large Loads, and identify a mechanism for recovering costs of complying with its obligations related to the Large Load Registry.  
Equinix argues that PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry lacks essential due process protections and that PJM may rely on registry data without requiring notice to affected customers, verification by those customers, or a meaningful correction mechanism.  Equinix states that this prevents customers from determining their IRAS obligations, undermines long-term procurement planning, and may force loads to commit to BYONC arrangements without assurance that the Large Load Registry’s treatment aligns with retail curtailment rules.  Industrial Customers request additional substantive and due process protections if existing Large Loads are included in the registry, including customer notice, correction, and appeal procedures and robust confidentiality safeguards for sensitive operational and commercial information.
Industrial Customers and IECA assert that existing large loads should be excluded from the proposed Large Load Registry to the extent it is used to implement IRAS; in their view, the Large Load Registry’s purpose is to track New Large Loads driving new system costs, not existing customers already integrated into the grid and reflected in historical forecasts.  Other parties, such as Joint Consumer Advocates and ODEC, raise confidentiality concerns with the registry.  ODEC seeks clarification from PJM as to whether LSEs will be required to provide Large Load Registry information, and is concerned that PJM’s proposal will require LSEs to provide information that they may not be able to obtain.  Joint Consumer Advocates claim that PJM’s proposal unreasonably restricts state consumer advocates’ access to the Large Load Registry, arguing entities with access are subject to onerous and insurmountable confidentiality restrictions.  Joint Consumer Advocates and Ohio Consumers’ Counsel argue that PJM should allow state consumer advocates access to the Large Load Registry because the information will play a central role in their advocacy efforts.  Pennsylvania Commission similarly states that it supports PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry, but requests that state utility commissions have access, and that the Large Load Registry should contain curtailment data.  OPSI and Ohio Consumers’ Counsel assert that states must have meaningful access to the registry so they can determine how curtailment should be implemented at the retail level and how resulting costs or responsibilities should be allocated consistent with state law and policy.  Similarly, Representative Pallone argues that the Large Load Registry, or as much of it as possible, must be public because it would be invaluable for improving forecasts of electricity demand.
The IMM argues that the proposed Large Load Registry, by itself, does not establish that PJM will receive real-time telemetry sufficient to monitor the load during an IRAS event, or to determine whether the required reduction action actually occurred.  The IMM contends that telemetry and performance measurement requirements are particularly important if IRAS reductions are to be treated as an operational reliability resource rather than merely as a forecasted or administrative load adjustment.  
In its answer, PJM highlights the importance of timely Commission approval of the Large Load Registry.  PJM states that the Commission has recognized that PJM must have visibility into where Large Loads will be located to be prepared for operational issues distinctive to Large Loads.  PJM states that there have been severe incidents of large loads tripping offline in PJM, which could have led to significant outages had PJM not been able to respond in time.  PJM asserts that such information will also be invaluable for states and other planning entities.
In response to states and state consumer advocates asserting that they should have broader, less-restricted access to the Large Load Registry, PJM asserts that the information contained in the Large Load Registry will be available to Authorized Commissions, among others, subject to confidentiality requirements.  PJM states that “Authorized Commission” is currently defined to include state public utility commissions, as well as organizations thereof.  PJM clarifies that the proposal does not recommend any new restrictions and that PJM plans to adhere to its existing rules for disseminating confidential information, as set forth in the Operating Agreement, and which the Commission approved many years ago.  PJM explains that the Large Load Registry is expected to collect information that may be confidential or commercially sensitive, or that may implicate infrastructure security concerns.  Therefore, PJM asserts, it must only permit access to this registry to “as small a universe of entities as possible,” while still making sure it is available to those who require access to implement their responsibilities, as well as operational and planning needs.  
In response to ODEC, PJM clarifies that it is the LSE serving a Large Load that is obligated to provide PJM with the information for the Large Load Registry, but acknowledges that there may be instances where an LSE may not have all the information required readily available, which is why the RAA language contemplates that the Electric Distributor may provide such information.  
In response to Industrial Customers and IECA’s arguments that the Large Load Registry should not include existing Large Loads, PJM states that, regardless of IRAS, PJM must have visibility into the full spectrum of all Large Loads in its footprint to properly manage its system and ensure reliability.
In their answers, Constellation and Google argue that the Commission should reject PJM’s proposal, other than the proposal to create the Large Load Registry.
FirstEnergy argues that PJM’s assertion that it does not presently perceive a connection between the Large Load Registry and the forthcoming pro forma transmission service agreement does not demonstrate that finalizing the Large Load Registry now will avoid overlapping, inconsistent, or duplicative requirements.
SMECO requests that the Commission direct PJM to conform proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section III(b) to PJM’s stated position that the LSE bears the Large Load Registry reporting obligation, and to clarify that an Electric Distributor that relays, in good faith, information originating with an LSE or Large Load is not responsible for the accuracy of that information.
Determination
We find that PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential because it will require LSEs to provide information about the Large Loads that they serve to PJM, which in turn will provide PJM with the information necessary to address the operational impacts of Large Loads on the PJM transmission system.  We agree with PJM that its proposed Large Load Registry will enable PJM to better forecast load growth and to plan and manage its transmission system.  We further find that the Large Load Registry will provide valuable information concerning—and visibility into—all Large Loads connecting to the PJM transmission system, separate and apart from implementation of PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.  Therefore, we sever PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry from the remainder of PJM’s proposal and accept it.  We direct PJM to submit a compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of this order, with the OATT and RAA provisions for the Large Load Registry, removing the language regarding the proposed IRAS and BYONC frameworks.
We also find just and reasonable PJM’s proposal to make information in the Large Load Registry available to Authorized Commissions, Transmission Owners, Electric Distributors, LSEs, the IMM, the Commission, and other entities, subject to appropriate confidentiality and data protection safeguards.  Some protesters express concern regarding the Large Load Registry information being subject to confidentiality restrictions.  We disagree with these parties and find that PJM’s proposal includes reasonable safeguards for confidential information.  PJM explains that the Large Load Registry will be available only to entities that already have access to this sort of information and consistent with existing confidentiality rules, i.e., PJM proposes to follow its existing, Commission-approved rules, rules that currently do not allow state consumer advocates or similar entities to have access to this type of information.  PJM further states that it will post only aggregated data on the PJM website, consistent with its existing confidentiality protections.  We find that PJM’s existing confidentiality rules and commitment to make only aggregate data publicly available will adequately safeguard confidential information submitted and maintained as part of the Large Load Registry, while balancing the need for broader transparency concerning Large Loads in the aggregate in PJM.
We disagree with protesters’ arguments that it is not reasonable for Electric Distributors to be responsible for the accuracy of the information in the Large Load Registry.  As PJM clarifies in its answer, the LSE serving a Large Load is obligated to provide PJM with the information for the Large Load Registry, and the Electric Distributor may provide information when the LSE does not have all the information required readily available.  With respect to SMECO’s concern that there is no mechanism for Electric Distributors to recover the costs of compliance, SMECO has not explained what costs it will incur, whether these are costs related to a wholesale service, or what information included in the Large Load Registry it would not otherwise already possess.  Also, given our findings elsewhere in this order, we expect that PJM will update the information that must be provided for inclusion in the registry to remove the previously identified items that are part of the IRAS package (such as the amount of BYONC brought by a particular Large Load).  Additionally, because we are rejecting PJM’s IRAS proposal, industrial customers will only be included in the Large Load Registry for informational purposes.  Similar to our finding concerning PJM’s proposed definition of Large Load in section III.B.1.a.iii above, we agree with PJM that it must have visibility into all Large Loads in the PJM Region to manage its system and ensure reliability.  Finally, as to commenters suggesting improvements to the Large Load Registry, we note that the Commission evaluates whether the proposal in the filing is just and reasonable, and not whether alternative proposals are more or less reasonable than the filing party’s proposal.
Given that, as discussed below, we are rejecting PJM’s proposed IRAS framework, we find that it is unnecessary to address protests arguing that the Large Load Registry is unjust and unreasonable because of how it is proposed to interact with IRAS.  For the same reason, we decline to address protests regarding telemetry or how the accuracy of the information in the Large Load Registry affects Eligible New Large Loads’ IRAS obligations.  We similarly find that it is unnecessary to address protests that states must have access to the Large Load Registry to determine curtailment and cost allocation given that, as discussed below, we are rejecting PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.
Interim Resource Adequacy Service Package
Although PJM asserts that its proposal can be viewed as containing discrete elements, we decline to sever the remaining aspects of the proposal because they appear to be an integrated package.  Below, we find that elements of the package are outside of the Commission’s jurisdiction or that PJM has not demonstrated that certain elements of the package are just and reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, including the proposed IRAS and BYONC frameworks.  As discussed below, we reject the entirety of the package.  
PJM’s Proposal
PJM proposes that, during years when the PJM Region experiences a resource adequacy shortfall, it may issue an IRAS Action directing Electric Distributors to reduce load attributable to Eligible New Large Loads in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area, unless the New Large Load is offset by new capacity through Reliability Backstop Procurement Unforced Capacity (UCAP) MW or BYONC arrangements.  PJM states that it may issue an IRAS Action when reserves or Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits cannot be maintained, and it “generally” would do so before Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions but after the deployment of available generation and economic demand resources, and curtailment of non-firm interchange and applicable non-firm transmission service.  Specifically, in the affidavit, Mr. Pilong explains that IRAS Actions would occur after PJM dispatchers have issued a NERC Energy Emergency Alert Level 1 (EEA1).  PJM states that IRAS would be suspended after three consecutive Delivery Years of PJM meeting its Reliability Requirements.  PJM proposes to set a maximum wholesale compensation rate for IRAS that is equal to 50% of the capacity performance Non-Performance Charge Rate, but the proposed Tariff states that the rate could be reduced if the Eligible New Large Load accepts in its retail rate a sum less than 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate or waives receipt of any compensation in its retail rate. 
Underpinning IRAS, PJM proposes a new obligation on LSEs that seek to procure NITS to support New Large Loads by designating new capacity resources in an amount at least equal to the load’s peak demand or such New Large Loads may be subject to curtailment under IRAS.  PJM also proposes to establish a new category of capacity resources, BYONC, that may be designated to address the needs of New Large Loads.  PJM states that BYONC would include new UCAP and eligible generation, storage, and eligible demand-side resources that satisfy gating criteria demonstrating their newness to the capacity market and PJM system, with UCAP fixed when the resource first clears.  PJM states that BYONC resources would remain subject to applicable capacity market obligations, including deficiency charges, performance penalties, plus a 10-year        must-offer requirement and $0/MW-day price-taker requirement, annual performance demonstrations for demand response and distributed energy resources, and a prohibition on external sales.  
Finally, beginning with the 2029/2030 Delivery Year, PJM proposes to exclude from the VRR curve New Large Load MW that has neither entered into BYONC arrangements nor received allocated Reliability Backstop Procurement UCAP MW, regardless of whether an IRAS-triggering shortfall exists.
Jurisdiction
PJM’s Filing
PJM argues that the proposed IRAS framework falls within the Commission’s established transmission jurisdiction and wholesale electricity jurisdiction.  PJM maintains that IRAS respects existing bright-line divisions between retail and wholesale jurisdiction over transmission and distribution.  According to PJM, IRAS represents a federal regime encouraging, but not mandating, states to re-evaluate load reduction plans, providing PJM the necessary tools to address situations where regional resource adequacy shortfalls would jeopardize reliability.  Moreover, PJM argues that it is preserving state authority by leaving retail load reduction and retail cost allocation to state-level entities, while offering non-mandatory options under the federal tariff to aid collection and settlement of compensation for IRAS.
PJM asserts that its proposal to direct the Electric Distributor, rather than a specific end-use customer, to reduce a quantity of load is in keeping with PJM’s longstanding practice and reflects the allocation of jurisdiction between the federal and state levels.  PJM states that it will not direct specific LSEs and/or specific customers of LSEs, including specific Large Loads, to reduce their load and/or switch to on-site back up resources; rather, those decisions would be worked out through state retail tariffs.  PJM asserts that this division of responsibility between PJM and the states and/or the Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (RERRA) is supported by precedent.  PJM asserts that states have exclusive jurisdiction to ensure the appropriate retail customers are reduced when IRAS Actions are called.  PJM argues that it may issue directives to Electric Distributors to reduce load by a certain MW quantity during certain, limited emergency conditions.  PJM states that while the amount attributable to each Electric Distributor zone/area will be guided by the Large Load Registry, PJM will leave it to Electric Distributors (in coordination with the states, LSEs, and LSE customers) to determine which loads should ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.  PJM argues the IRAS framework divides authority between PJM and the states in a manner consistent with the FPA’s basic division of authority.
PJM also argues that this is not an improper delegation of federal authority to the states because the division of responsibility reflected in the Tariff would be on file and remain subject to the Commission’s authority.  PJM asserts that its resource adequacy framework recognizes the traditional role of state and local entities, and that the Commission has found that the appropriate course of action has been to defer to state and local entities’ decisions when possible while not shirking its responsibility under the FPA.
PJM likewise argues that its compensation framework respects and reflects the federal and state division of authority.  PJM asserts that the IRAS rate is compensation for a wholesale load reduction service.  However, PJM also asserts that the rate is intended to be conjoined with retail rates and that the entities to be paid the rate and the loads to be charged to support such compensation must be determined at the state level.  PJM argues that the net result is a reduced capacity charge for the Eligible New Large Load, and thus is a practice that directly affects wholesale capacity rates assessed.  PJM states that, while it enlists or invites state action through their jurisdictional retail process, it does not mandate any state-specific action, nor does it require any specific terms and conditions on retail service.  Rather, PJM asserts that its proposed filed rate facilitates and respects the handoff of responsibilities between federal wholesale rate development and state retail rate development.  PJM states that, like demand response rules, this framework respects state law choices about whether and how to facilitate implementation of a wholesale paradigm.
Pleadings
Many protesters argue that PJM’s proposal impermissibly intrudes on state authority by directly regulating retail customers, contrary to section 201(b) of the FPA.  They argue that decisions regarding retail service, rates, and curtailment priorities are reserved for states and local regulators.  Protesters assert that the customers proposed to be curtailed are retail customers and the compensation will be collected from and paid to retail customers.  Protesters assert that PJM’s proposal contains several triggers that “target” specific retail customers by conditioning curtailment on retail characteristics, such as size, vintage, and whether the retail customer brings offsetting new capacity.  Protesters also assert that the proposal does not directly affect wholesale rates.  
Protesters contend that PJM’s assertion that it is only imposing curtailment obligations on Electric Distributors does not alleviate the jurisdictional intrusion.  Further, some protesters argue that the operative Tariff language places obligations directly on New Large Loads.  Protesters assert that assigning curtailment to Electric Distributors merely makes them conduits for PJM’s retail-focused directives, leaving states powerless. Protesters assert that PJM’s use of Electric Distributors demonstrates that PJM is doing indirectly what it cannot do directly.  Protesters also assert that demand response participation rules and Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.’s Expedited Resource Addition Study are not analogous to IRAS because those programs addressed only wholesale market compensation for voluntary participation, where states permit such participation. 
Protesters also assert that PJM’s proposal impermissibly compels states to implement a federal program.  Specifically, they argue that PJM is pressuring states to conform by deferring key curtailment and compensation decisions to state and local authorities, requiring the creation of new programs or retail tariff changes, and imposing obligations on Electric Distributors without clear state oversight.
Protesters also argue that the IRAS compensation framework establishes a retail rate.  For example, Constellation asserts that PJM sets compensation and requires Electric Distributors to pay that amount by assessing charges against retail customers in their zone/area to pay other retail customers.  West Virginia Commission warns that West Virginia’s tools for setting retail rates for uncovered New Large Load could be challenged if the Commission approved PJM’s wholesale compensation for those New Large Loads that do not voluntarily turn down compensation.  
Several protesters also argue that the proposal impermissibly delegates authority to set the Commission-jurisdictional wholesale rate to states.  They contend that PJM’s proposal leaves compensation and curtailment decisions to state-regulated entities, making the wholesale rate unclear and effectively set by the states rather than the Commission.
On the other hand, certain commenters assert that the proposal generally respects the division of state and federal authority under the FPA.  They argue that the proposal falls squarely within PJM’s authority to maintain resource adequacy at the wholesale level.  PIOs note that the FPA does not prohibit rules that indirectly affect retail customer behavior.  PIOs explain that PJM has a specific and limited role with no direct control over retail end-use customers and that IRAS Actions will be implemented through Electric Distributors at the wholesale level.  PIOs assert that PJM will rely on aggregate MW quantities of load and supply to implement IRAS and that, while it will track retail customers, it will act at the macro level using aggregate quantities by zone.  Appalachian Voices likewise asserts that PJM’s proposal operates within the Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission service and bulk power system reliability, and that tying the MW quantity to be shed to New Large Loads is a matter of reliability and cost causation.  The IMM argues that PJM’s proposal does not go far enough; it asserts that PJM has authority to curtail individual Large Loads and should not abdicate the responsibility to set and implement the terms and conditions of curtailment to the Electric Distributor and/or states.
Governor Shapiro argues that IRAS is a supplemental wholesale capacity product designed to ensure the reliability of the bulk power system, which is within PJM’s jurisdiction.  Governor Shapiro states that the Operating Agreement already grants PJM the ability to coordinate curtailment of load where PJM determines the aggregate amount of MW load reduction required to be curtailed and the Transmission Owner or Electric Distributor determines which end-use entities are curtailed.  Governor Shapiro argues that IRAS differs from this pre-existing authority in two ways, neither of which impact jurisdiction:  (1) curtailment direction takes place prior to EEA1; and (2) the means by which PJM determines the aggregate MW of load to be curtailed in a zone or area.  Governor Shapiro states that implementing IRAS Actions prior to EEA1 will avoid escalating emergency procedures that would impose financial and reliability costs caused by Large Loads on all customers.  Governor Shapiro states that, while PJM determines aggregate MW reductions within a zone based on that zone’s share of New Large Loads, PJM does not direct the curtailment of loads, and that it remains up to the retail authority to implement the retail end-user priority.  Governor Shapiro argues that it is appropriate for PJM to focus on non-capacity backed New Large Loads when determining aggregate MW reduction targets, as it is those entities that are causing the reliability emergency, and is consistent with requirements in the Operating Agreement that PJM not order a load shed in one zone to address deficiencies in another zone.  Governor Shapiro argues that protesters acknowledge that PJM’s proposal does not target specific retail customers.
Governor Shapiro argues that there is no merit to the position that PJM is legally barred from acting on information about characteristics of load growth in a zone when that information is directly relevant to the operation of the bulk power system.  Governor Shapiro states that case law has never imposed such strict boundaries, that the characteristics of retail loads and generation are highly relevant to informing a wholesale rate, and that taking this information into account when setting wholesale rates does not constitute regulation of those matters.  Governor Shapiro states that, if this position were to be adopted, both the Commission and PJM would be barred from considering information about generating facilities when setting wholesale rates, because neither the Commission nor PJM may directly regulate generation.  Governor Shapiro argues that this jurisdictional position would be unworkable if applied to generation and is equally so if applied to retail loads.
As to the compensation framework, Governor Shapiro asserts that, although PJM “confusingly” appears to speak about compensation that would be provided to individual retail customers, because PJM will only direct a MW quantity to be curtailed, wholesale compensation will therefore accrue as a credit on a wholesale bill to the wholesale customers based on that total MW quantity of load curtailment.  Governor Shapiro acknowledges that PJM could clean up the proposed Tariff provisions related to IRAS compensation to (1) remove all references to “Eligible New Large Loads” to clarify that it is setting a wholesale rate; and (2) clarify that the particular level of compensation depends on certain conditions, which inform the implementation of and are an input into the wholesale rate. 
In its answer, PJM asserts that IRAS is targeted at improving the wholesale market by supporting resource adequacy and reliability, which directly affects Commission jurisdictional rates.  PJM argues that IRAS operates within PJM’s authority to require load reduction under real-time conditions that may give rise to system instability or capacity shortfalls.  PJM argues that IRAS may ultimately affect retail customers but does not present an impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation because the proposal places the terms and conditions on LSEs, not end-use retail customers.  PJM reiterates that it will only determine the quantity of load to be curtailed by Electric Distributors, that it will leave to the states to determine which resources will be called upon to reduce load, and that it will not determine whether any specific retail customer is called upon to reduce load or whether any load may say no to such a directive.  PJM contends that protesters make contradictory claims that IRAS imposes mandatory rules on end-use retail customers, but also that IRAS leaves too much discretion to states to determine which entities are curtailed. 
PJM likewise argues that its compensation mechanism targets wholesale rates for wholesale customers and is not an attempt to create a retail compensation scheme for curtailed large loads or an impermissible delegation to states of its wholesale ratemaking authority.  PJM explains that IRAS compensation neither mandates state-specific action nor imposes specific terms and conditions on retail rates.  Instead, PJM asserts that it is using its authority to set rates for operational actions to reduce energy consumption as part of the Commission’s wholesale jurisdiction, with all other aspects of ratemaking, including application of that rate to different retail customer classes, left to the states.  PJM states that, just like wholesale demand response participation depends on state permission, wholesale compensation for IRAS at a reduced level depends on RERRA action specifying an alternative compensation below the maximum rate.  Furthermore, PJM states that the Tariff contemplates that entities to be paid the rate and the loads to be charged to support such compensation are determined at the state level.
In its answer, Google asserts that when it comes to determining whether a rate is jurisdictionally permissible under the FPA, the dispositive question is how it works in practice, not the relevant public utility’s transmittal letter.  Constellation and Data Center Coalition argue that the express language of the proposed Tariff unlawfully targets and requires curtailment of a specific category of retail customers, i.e., Eligible New Large Loads, thereby regulating the terms of retail service and intruding on state jurisdiction.  Specifically, Constellation and Data Center Coalition cite the proposed Tariff, which states that “Electric Distributors” shall “execute the [PJM] Office of the Interconnection’s directives to implement Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions among the Eligible New Large Loads in the Electric Distributor’s zone/area.”  Constellation asserts that the proposed Tariff language leaves no doubt that Electric Distributors would actually violate the PJM Tariff if they bypassed curtailment of Eligible New Large Loads and chose to curtail other retail customers instead.  
Constellation, Data Center Coalition, FirstEnergy, Google, and Vistra further argue that the Tri-State order does not support PJM’s proposal because, unlike the accepted Tri-State tariff, PJM’s proposed Tariff leaves Electric Distributors no discretion to determine whether and how retail customers will be affected.
Constellation also argues that the answers fail to explain how the proposal’s compensation provisions target wholesale rates when they effectively set retail compensation for interrupted service, making them jurisdictionally improper.  Constellation contends that, even if the compensation is wholesale, the proposal impermissibly gives states direct authority to set or vary wholesale compensation, unlike Order No. 719’s permissible deference to state preferences.
Constellation argues, in response to answers’ claims that IRAS is no different from PJM’s existing curtailment authority and falls within the Commission’s and states’ resource adequacy powers, that the proposal instead creates a novel curtailment regime based on retail customer characteristics and rates that requires jurisdictionally proper action.
PPL argues that it is not clear in PJM’s proposal and Tariff language that state regulatory authorities have the power to opt-out individual Eligible New Large Loads from the requirement to provide IRAS.  Specifically, PPL argues that it is unclear under what legal authority state regulatory authorities in the PJM Region would be able to compel end-use retail customers (Eligible New Large Loads) to provide a Commission-jurisdictional wholesale service to PJM.  PPL asserts that states lack authority to compel end-use retail customers to provide Commission-jurisdictional wholesale services to PJM, and that doing so would be an unprecedented and constitutionally problematic intrusion into the Commission’s plenary jurisdiction under the FPA.  PPL suggests that PJM either (1) have the Tariff language stop at the issuance of the Operating Instruction to Electric Distributors to curtail load, and leave the rates, terms, and conditions of that load curtailment service to state and local regulatory authorities; or (2) make IRAS a voluntary Commission-jurisdictional service, whereby Electric Distributors and/or Large Load customers themselves can choose whether to participate like any other wholesale market service provider in PJM.
The IMM argues that, although the IRAS proposal is within the Commission’s jurisdiction, PJM’s proposal fails to establish consistent regional curtailment rules and relies on states to complete the proposal.  The IMM argues that Data Center Coalition’s assertion that data centers’ status as retail customers prevents PJM from imposing wholesale-market capacity and curtailment requirements is inconsistent with the Commission’s recognized jurisdiction over retail customers’ participation in wholesale markets and with the RAA’s existing requirements for LSEs to procure qualifying capacity.  
Determination
We find that certain aspects of PJM’s proposal appear to present an impermissible intrusion on retail rate regulation and are not subject to the Commission’s authority pursuant to section 205 of the FPA.  We find that several provisions of the proposed Tariff appear to place obligations directly on Eligible New Large Loads, which are, for the most part, retail customers; that certain other provisions appear to dictate which retail customers taking retail service will be curtailed; and that the proposed compensation framework appears to establish a retail rate.  Therefore, we reject PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.
The FPA authorizes the Commission to regulate “rates, terms, and conditions” and any “rule, regulation, practice, or contract” directly “affecting” such transmission or wholesale rates.  But the law places beyond the Commission’s jurisdiction, and leaves to the states alone, the regulation of “any other sale”—most notably, any retail sale—of electricity.  Section 201 of the FPA further limits the Commission’s jurisdiction to “those matters which are not subject to regulation by the states.” 
In EPSA, the U.S. Supreme Court stated that although “the wholesale and retail markets in electricity are inextricably linked,” the Commission “may not regulate . . . retail sales of electricity.”  The Court further stated that “no matter how direct, or dramatic” a proposal’s impact on wholesale rates, the Commission may not regulate retail electricity sales.  The Court also clarified that the FPA limits the Commission’s jurisdiction to wholesale sales, reserving regulatory authority over retail sales to the states alone, and that any regulation that “specifies terms of sale at retail” exceeds the Commission’s authority under the FPA.  
In the instant proceeding, protesters argue that PJM is proposing, via a Commission-jurisdictional tariff, terms of retail service for Eligible New Large Loads.  These protesters contend that PJM is doing so by placing obligations on Eligible New Large Loads, which are, for the most part, retail customers taking retail service; by dictating which retail customers an Electric Distributor must curtail; and by establishing the compensation for Eligible New Large Loads.  PJM’s proposed construct appears to regulate the terms and conditions of a retail customer’s service in ways that are beyond the Commission’s authority.  
First, the proposed Tariff appears to direct specific retail customers to provide IRAS for wholesale service and, therefore, to curtail.  For example, IRAS is defined as “a load reduction service through which New Large Loads reduce load as directed by the applicable Electric Distributor in response to an [IRAS] Action requested by [PJM].”  The IRAS Tariff provisions also state that the Electric Distributor “shall” implement the curtailment among “Eligible New Large Loads” and therefore specifies the class of retail customers that should be curtailed.  Further, the proposed Tariff states that when IRAS is suspended, “[PJM] does not need any Eligible New Large Loads to be available to provide [IRAS] for that Delivery Year.”  Eligible New Large Loads are, for the most part, retail customers taking retail service.  PJM’s transmittal seems to recognize this, proposing that IRAS MWs be assigned to Electric Distributors, with the state/RERRAs responsible for identifying which loads will be obligated to curtail under IRAS.  As such, PJM’s transmittal states that its proposed Tariff imposes obligations only on the Electric Distributor by assigning curtailment obligations to Electric Distributors, who can then, at the direction of retail regulators, determine which retail customers are curtailed.  While the proposal described in PJM’s transmittal may be within the Commission’s jurisdiction, we find that the plain language of the Tariff, as proposed, appears to place obligations directly on the Eligible New Large Loads and requires Electric Distributors to curtail the Eligible New Large Loads.  We note that PJM’s answer fails to engage with the concern that its proposal, as described in its transmittal, is inconsistent with the proposed Tariff’s plain language that imposes obligations directly on Eligible New Large Loads and requires Electric Distributors to curtail Eligible New Large Loads.  
Second, the proposed Tariff appears to be setting a retail rate because it establishes a compensation rate for IRAS payable to the Eligible New Large Load.  The proposed Tariff directs compensation at Eligible New Large Loads, which are, for the most part, retail customers taking retail service.  The proposed Tariff also appears to specify that retail customers will be charged to fund such compensation.  The proposed Tariff language thus appears to establish a framework whereby retail customers will be paid by other retail customers for what PJM describes as a wholesale capacity service.  Although Governor Shapiro asserts that the wholesale customer would receive a credit, and PJM asserts in its answer that the LSE would be compensated for load reduction, this is not specified anywhere in the proposed Tariff language.  The proposed Tariff does not specify what wholesale customer would be paid for IRAS or how; it only mentions payment to the Electric Distributor’s customers, who are retail customers.  Nor is payment guaranteed under PJM’s proposal, as PJM only proposes a default rate that appears subject to further change and beyond the reach of the Tariff.  Furthermore, while PJM’s transmittal recognizes that the retail entities to be paid the rate and the loads charged for the rate must be set by state regulators, protesters like the Virginia Commission highlight that the proposed Tariff does not include any language stating that retail regulators may establish the rate.  Instead, the proposed Tariff indicates that the New Large Load may elect to reduce or waive its compensation for IRAS.  Accordingly, we find that the proposed Tariff appears to impermissibly set a retail rate.    
Finally, the proposed Tariff also appears to allow the Electric Distributor, which PJM’s transmittal explains would occur in consultation with the RERRA, to determine which customers will pay the compensation to the entities providing IRAS pursuant to the PJM Tariff and the level of compensation, which we interpret as allowing a retail regulator to set a wholesale rate. 
Undue Discrimination – IRAS Curtailment
PJM’s Filing
PJM asserts that its proposal is not unduly discriminatory or preferential because the IRAS framework recognizes that New Large Loads are not similarly situated to other loads.  To support this conclusion, PJM states that members of Congress have expressed to PJM that “[i]t is not unduly discriminatory to identify and manage demand from new data centers given their incomparably large energy demands, how quickly data centers can come online, and their unique potential to impact the reliability of the electric grid as a collective class and to increase rates for all customers.”  Further, PJM states that New Large Loads constitute a separate, new class of load, and are therefore appropriately subject to different treatment.  PJM asserts that New Large Loads are not similarly situated to other loads in the PJM Region because, according to the Commission, large loads constitute “a separate category of load.”  Additionally, PJM states that the Commission has highlighted the uniqueness of large loads, noting specifically that their integration “poses specific challenges to transmission system operation given their size, operational behavior, and unique potential to impact the transmission system.”  
Similarly, PJM points to the Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (CHILLS) order, where the Commission found that the proposal for new large loads was just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  PJM states that the Commission observed that “SPP has shown that unprecedented growth in large loads in the SPP region presents significant and unique operational and planning challenges.”  PJM states that in the last two Delivery Years, since the influx of new large loads consisting primarily of data centers, PJM has cleared short of its PJM Region Reliability Requirement in the face of exponential load growth.
Pleadings
Protesters generally argue that IRAS is unduly discriminatory because it treats Large Loads, and/or the LSE or Electric Distributor serving them, differently on the basis of the retail customer’s size, vintage, or capacity procurement.  This disparate treatment, they contend, is not justified by the actual impact these customers have on system reliability, nor does PJM demonstrate material differences relevant to reliability or resource adequacy.  Specifically, protesters assert that PJM has not demonstrated that the size or in-service date is relevant to the load’s impact on reliability or capacity because the capacity of the system is burdened in the same way by a new or existing large load, and by a single new large load or many new smaller loads.  Some protesters also assert that these characteristics are not material because existing or smaller new loads can also procure capacity and provide the same curtailment.
Some protesters argue that PJM’s proposal unduly discriminates against LSEs taking NITS on behalf of New Large Loads, as compared to LSEs taking NITS on behalf of other new loads.  Constellation and the Data Center Coalition argue that PJM’s proposal unfairly creates a subclass of NITS customers—those serving Eligible New Large Loads—who pay the same transmission and capacity rates as other NITS customers but receive inferior service and are subject to involuntary curtailment ahead of other firm customers.  The Data Center Coalition further argues that PJM’s proposal undermines traditional curtailment priority of NITS customers, effectively turning them into second-class customers by depriving them of equal protection from service interruptions and equal curtailment treatment.  Protesters contend that PJM’s rationale for disparate treatment based on Large Loads is arbitrary and unsupported, and that similarly situated NITS customers should receive comparable service and rates, rather than being subject to unduly discriminatory and preferential treatment.  
Some protesters also argue that PJM’s proposal unduly discriminates against Electric Distributors with LSEs serving Eligible New Large Loads in their zone/area as compared to Electric Distributors that do not have LSEs serving Eligible New Large Loads in their zone/area.  They further contend that retail customer characteristics are not a relevant distinction for resource adequacy challenges.  Vistra argues that the consideration relevant to resource adequacy is instead whether an Electric Distributor is generation deficient.  Google likewise asserts that the relevant factor that causes the resource adequacy challenge is aggregate load growth in a zone/area, not the load growth of only a subset of customers.
Other commenters assert that differential treatment is not undue because the size and operational characteristics of New Large Loads create unique concerns for resource adequacy, reliability, and affordability, and so New Large Loads, and the entities that serve them, are not similarly situated.  PIOs assert that New Large Loads are different from traditional residential and commercial load because they grow rapidly and unpredictably with concentrated impacts on the electricity system, and develop significantly faster than construction of new supply.  PIOs argue that as such, New Large Loads pose distinct challenges for reliability and affordability.  PIOs argue that New Large Loads are having an outsized impact on future resource adequacy and on   real-time reliability, which warrants placing unique requirements on them through LSEs and Electric Distributors.  Appalachian Voices likewise argues that the distinction is based on legitimate operational constraints caused by the sudden and unexpected influx of New Large Load demand, which has significantly higher demand requirements and higher load factors.
In its answer, PJM reiterates that IRAS is not unduly discriminatory because of the unique characteristics of Large Loads that are relevant to ensuring just and reasonable rates and the reliable operation of the bulk power system.  PJM further asserts that IRAS is narrowly tailored to address capacity shortfalls caused by New Large Loads that lack sufficient capacity and applies only during specifically defined emergency situations.  PJM also argues that distinguishing between existing Large Loads and New Large Loads based on vintage is justified because new, rather than existing, load causes the capacity shortfall that necessitates IRAS. 
In their answers, Constellation, Data Center Coalition, and Vistra argue that parties do not explain why New Large Loads are solely or disproportionately responsible for the region’s resource adequacy shortfall.  They assert that both new and existing Large Loads contribute to the resource adequacy shortfall because every transmission system user is economically marginal.  Data Center Coalition and Vistra also argue that PJM misread the SPP CHILLS precedent, which they argue supports offering different services to differently situated loads but not reducing NITS for Electric Distributors serving materially identical loads.
Constellation further argues that Governor Shapiro’s justification for discriminating against new large computational loads highlights, rather than resolves, the proposal’s unlawfulness because it fails to explain why those loads differ in their capacity needs or resource adequacy burdens, and conflicts with PJM’s rejection of distinctions between computational and other large loads.
The IMM disagrees with Data Center Coalition that IRAS is unduly discriminatory because the IMM argues that data centers uniquely drive PJM’s reliability challenges through their rapid, large-scale interconnection requests and reliance on curtailments before the necessary infrastructure is available, making data center specific rules consistent with cost-causation principles.
Determination
We find that PJM has not currently offered sufficiently detailed evidence concerning how its treatment of Electric Distributors and LSEs taking NITS differently in the resource adequacy context based on the characteristics of their retail customers is not unduly discriminatory.  PJM’s proposal imposes capacity procurement and curtailment obligations on Electric Distributors and LSEs taking NITS to serve certain loads based on retail customer characteristics, yet PJM has not at this time produced evidence sufficient to demonstrate how such characteristics are material to the resource adequacy challenges its proposal seeks to address.  Historically, PJM’s capacity market has treated all load taking NITS comparably, procuring capacity on its behalf regardless of retail customer class or whether the load is new or existing.  While PJM now proposes to distinguish between different loads taking NITS on these bases for purposes of both procuring capacity through its Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) and curtailing NITS, it fails to provide sufficiently detailed evidence to support why Electric Distributors and LSEs using NITS to serve New Large Loads should not be treated comparably to Electric Distributors and LSEs using NITS to serve equivalent quantities of load growth.  We note PJM’s explanation that New Large Loads have unique characteristics compared to traditional load growth and are the primary cause for the resource adequacy shortfall, assertions with which some commenters agree, but we find that PJM’s generic references to these retail customer characteristics without more detail are insufficient evidence to counter the current resource adequacy construct in PJM, i.e., that PJM will procure sufficient capacity to serve all NITS load in the PJM Region.  Therefore, we find that, in its current filing, PJM did not adequately support its proposal to treat Electric Distributors and LSEs differently based on the characteristics of their retail customers.
Should PJM choose to refile a modified version of its proposed IRAS framework, we encourage PJM to either provide further justification regarding its proposed treatment of Electric Distributors or LSEs using NITS to serve New Large Loads or revise its proposal to not expressly single out LSEs using NITS to serve New Large Loads, or Electric Distributors on the basis of the amount of New Large Loads in its zones/areas.
