As we have previously stated, we recognize that the rapid emergence of large loads presents a shared regulatory challenge that implicates both federal and state authority.  States have a crucial role to play in this challenge by designating which retail customers must be curtailed when the system is stressed, and we strongly encourage states to continue their important work on this issue.
BYONC Accreditation
PJM’s Filing
PJM proposes that New Large Loads can avoid curtailment under IRAS by bringing new capacity to offset their capacity needs.  PJM states that BYONC resources will be subject to all of the requirements for capacity resources associated with their resource type, including deficiency charges and capacity performance penalties.  PJM proposes that:  (1) a BYONC resource’s UCAP level be determined in the first auction it clears; and (2) BYONC resources are subject to a 10-year must-offer and $0/MW-Day offer requirement in PJM’s capacity market, including resource types usually exempt from the must-offer requirement, such as demand response resources.  Demand response and distributed energy resources will be required to demonstrate their performance each year of the 10-year period consistent with those resource classes’ treatment in the capacity market.  
PJM explains that the timing of the BYONC arrangement is central to the determination of the BYONC’s Accredited UCAP value because the ICAP equivalent of the Accredited UCAP value is used to reduce a New Large Load’s potential IRAS availability.
Pleadings
AMP requests that the Commission direct PJM to modify its proposal to set the level of BYONC for a generation or storage resource at the resource’s accredited capacity in the first year it is in arrangement with a New Large Load.  AMP argues PJM expects the Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) of some resource classes, especially storage, to decline over the BYONC commitment term, and using a fixed ELCC value for BYONC would therefore over-credit New Large Loads for BYONC.  AMP argues that the portion of the New Large Load that exceeds the ELCC-measured UCAP of the supporting BYONC resource is effectively the same as Eligible New Large Load but without the IRAS obligation.
Further, AMP argues that PJM has not explained how BYONC will be accredited for the purposes of the RPM.  AMP states that, if the fixed Accredited UCAP is used, and exceeds the UCAP that would have resulted from applying updated ELCC values to the underlying resources, PJM would be counting and clearing MW of Accredited UCAP that may not exist.  However, AMP continues, if the Accredited UCAP of BYONC resources is updated for the RPM, the BYONC MW in the RPM could be less than the MW of New Large Loads, potentially shifting costs to other customers.  
EPSA and FirstEnergy assert that the proposal to lock in the BYONC resource’s accreditation grants BYONC resources unduly preferential treatment under ELCC accreditation.  EPSA similarly argues that the lock-in mechanism may result in a BYONC’s capacity contribution being overstated in RPM Auctions, which will further erode the fidelity of the RPM BRA or incremental auction price signal.  The IMM argues that it is unjust and unreasonable to protect new generation from ELCC risk.  The IMM explains that, regardless of the technology, fixing the accredited UCAP at a single value over the period will misrepresent the actual UCAP.  AEU supports the lock-in mechanism, asserting that this prevents resources from being exposed to unhedgeable ELCC risk.
In its answer, PJM argues that IRAS is intended to incent New Large Loads to bring new capacity to meet their resource adequacy needs, and asserts that the lock-in mechanism avoids introducing uncertainty to the BYONC arrangement and undermining the BYONC incentive.  PJM asserts that “the risk of changes to ELCC values (both increases and decreases) remains just as it is today—on individual generators in the first instance and all customers in the event that PJM has to purchase more capacity due to an aggregate ELCC decline.” 
The IMM argues that disregarding changes in actual ELCC values does not eliminate uncertainty; it shifts the risks of any capacity shortfall, and the cost of procuring additional capacity, to other PJM customers.
Determination
We find that PJM has not sufficiently justified its proposal to lock in the accreditation of BYONC resources over the lifetime of the BYONC arrangement to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Generation resources vary considerably in their operating characteristics, including various fuel types, dispatchability, and maximum run times.  UCAP accreditation, as implemented through PJM’s ELCC, is designed to create a single tradeable capacity product from a field of diverse and distinct generation resources.  We find that PJM has failed to provide sufficient record evidence to substantiate its rationale for allowing BYONC resources to provide capacity when that capacity is not equivalent to the single tradable capacity product that PJM procures through its RPM because its accreditation value is fixed over the term of the BYONC arrangement.  This lack of substantiation is heightened by the fact that PJM’s proposed Tariff language and its description of the lock-in arrangement are inconsistent.
Specifically, PJM states that the lock-in period acts as a “shield” to BYONC resources from changes in their capacity accreditation (as determined through PJM’s ELCC capacity accreditation method) by locking in their accreditation for the period of the BYONC arrangement.  While, in its answer, PJM contends that locking in a BYONC resource’s capacity accreditation will provide certainty to a New Large Load contracting with a BYONC resource and incentivize parties to enter into BYONC arrangements, PJM also asserts that “the risk of changes to ELCC values (both increases and decreases) remains just as it is today—on individual generators in the first instance and all customers in the event that PJM has to purchase more capacity due to an aggregate ELCC decline.”  Yet, despite PJM’s assertion in its answer, PJM’s proposed Tariff provides that the “Accredited UCAP of any BYONC shall be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared for the initial Delivery Year . . . .”  We find that PJM has not sufficiently demonstrated that the potential benefits of locking in BYONC resources’ capacity accreditation outweigh PJM’s obligation to ensure that the PJM Region’s resource adequacy needs are met.  
With respect to the arguments PJM has offered, we are concerned with whether PJM’s lock-in Tariff language proposal may worsen the problems it is attempting to solve.  Specifically, PJM’s proposal to lock in the accreditation value of BYONC resources may also risk the capacity market procuring too little or too much capacity should the BYONC resource’s actual ELCC accreditation fall or rise over time.  While PJM contends that the risk of the ELCC accreditation decreasing will still lie with individual capacity resources in the first instance, that statement does not appear to hold with respect to BYONC resources, whose accreditation value will be locked in for the term of the BYONC arrangement per the proposed Tariff language.  We agree with PJM that whenever ELCC accreditation declines, it will affect all load because PJM will have to procure additional capacity.  However, the risk that a BYONC resource’s    locked-in accreditation value be higher than the capacity that it can actually provide has the potential to create a new resource adequacy risk for the entire PJM Region, particularly given the potential magnitude of BYONC MW that will be offered into and clear the capacity market.  We note PJM’s explanation that the lock-in mechanism would avoid introducing uncertainty to the BYONC arrangement that would undermine the incentive for Large Loads to contract with new capacity.  However, PJM has not sufficiently substantiated in the current record—especially with the conflicting Tariff language and explanation—that those considerations outweigh the potential downsides of introducing new resource adequacy risks and therefore merit a different approach to ELCC accreditation for BYONC resources.  For these reasons, we find that PJM has not sufficiently substantiated that its proposal to lock in the value of BYONC UCAP accreditation is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. 
Other Issues
Because we are rejecting PJM’s proposed IRAS framework, which as noted above appears to be an integrated package, we need not address other issues raised in this proceeding regarding the merits of other aspects of IRAS.  However, we note that several elements of PJM’s proposed IRAS framework (including but not limited to those discussed below) may require additional justification to demonstrate that they are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Should PJM choose to refile a modified version of its proposed IRAS framework that does not infringe on retail rate regulation, we encourage PJM to address the concerns discussed below.
First, we are concerned that, as designed, PJM’s proposal may not be consistent with mandatory Reliability Standards.  Reliability Standard EOP-011-4 only permits firm loads to be curtailed following initiation by the reliability coordinator of an EEA3, which is when “[t]he energy deficient Balancing Authority is unable to meet minimum Contingency Reserve requirements.”  In contrast, PJM’s proposal would direct Electric Distributors to curtail certain load, which comprise a portion of a Transmission Customer’s firm NITS load under PJM’s proposal, earlier in the emergency process, at EEA1, when all generation is committed and non-firm wholesale energy sales have been curtailed.  Although firm loads willing to receive a lower curtailment priority, such as demand response resources, may be voluntarily curtailed before EEA3 under the mandatory Reliability Standards, PJM’s proposal would shed firm load on an involuntary basis.  Several parties argue that it is not just and reasonable to curtail IRAS MW before demand response resources.  Others argue that curtailing New Large Loads prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management is just and reasonable.  Nevertheless, PJM has crafted curtailment rules that do not appear internally consistent with its Tariff (i.e., curtailing certain transmission customers on a pro rata basis).  It appears that PJM’s proposal ignores the plain language of mandatory Reliability Standard EOP-011-4 regarding the curtailment priority of loads for whom an Eligible Customer is taking and paying for firm transmission service, which would result in PJM dispatch actions that conflict with the mandatory Reliability Standards.  
Second, the current record suggests that the LSE using NITS to serve an Eligible New Large Load would be required to pay the same capacity charges and transmission charges as LSEs using NITS to serve other types of load that are not subject to curtailment under IRAS and on whose behalf PJM procures capacity.  Protesters argue that LSEs should not be allocated capacity charges based on the MW of Eligible New Large Loads when PJM has excluded such loads from the VRR curve, and is therefore not procuring capacity for said loads, or when these loads will be curtailed before capacity resources that are demand response resources are deployed.  It appears that PJM has not sufficiently justified why it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential for LSEs using NITS to serve Eligible New Large Loads to be charged for capacity based on the quantity of Eligible New Large Load MW when PJM does not procure capacity on behalf of that load.  The Commission has previously found that Eligible Customers taking non-firm transmission service on behalf of co-located load should not be charged for capacity because PJM does not procure capacity on their behalf.  We are concerned that PJM has not adequately explained why it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential to diverge from this principle.  
Third, we are concerned that PJM’s proposal does not take into account locational or deliverability considerations for BYONC resources.  We note that under PJM’s existing Tariff, PJM identifies LDA Reliability Requirements, which require sufficient capacity to be inside or deliverable to the LDA based on transmission constraints.  Under PJM’s proposal, the New Large Load would not be subject to IRAS, and its load would not be counted towards the Eligible New Large Load amount for its EDC zone/area, regardless of transmission constraints between the New Large Load and the BYONC resource, which could exacerbate the resource adequacy shortfall in the New Large Load’s zone.  If PJM chooses to file a new proposal, PJM may consider if it is appropriate to condition IRAS consideration of BYONC arrangements on PJM finding that the BYONC resources are deliverable to the LDAs where the New Large Loads with which they are in agreements are located.
Fourth, the record suggests that PJM’s designation of New Large Loads to provide IRAS obligations may disrupt existing commercial arrangements, including binding agreements between large loads that will ramp up after June 1, 2027 and existing generation.  Should PJM choose to refile, PJM should consider how to account for or acknowledge these concerns, to the extent they persist given our other findings and guidance in this order.  It also appears that PJM has not adequately explained why a threshold only on the overall size of the Large Load, and not on the incremental increase of an existing Large Load, is just and reasonable.  The proposed Tariff appears to treat existing NITS customers differently even on the basis of small MW increases, such that a 49 MW existing load that increased its consumption by 1 MW would become a 50 MW New Large Load and impose new requirements on the existing NITS customer for the entire 50 MW.  Should PJM choose to file a new proposal, we encourage PJM to clarify exactly how the definition of New Large Load and any IRAS or IRAS-like framework would apply to such existing commercial arrangements.  The proposed Tariff also does not appear to account for existing Behind the Meter Generation rules, although the Commission has found that NITS customers may net up to 50 MW of load at a particular electrical location using Behind the Meter Generation.  
We also note that the new non-firm transmission services proposed in the order to show cause proceeding on co-located load—specifically Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service—demonstrate a concept that PJM could consider as another possible avenue to achieve some of the aims of PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.  In the PJM Large Load Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily found that PJM’s Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it does not include transmission services that reflect Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of flexible large loads that are willing and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.  The Commission directed PJM to explain whether its Tariff remains just and reasonable without Non-Firm Contract Demand Service for flexible large loads.  It appears that a non-firm transmission service similar to Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service, with appropriate adjustments, might be considered as a potential avenue to achieve some of the aims of PJM’s proposed IRAS framework.  However, we note that Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is affirmatively a voluntary option, while the product or service here is not.  Should PJM choose to refile its IRAS proposal, we encourage PJM to clearly identify the product or service IRAS is intended to provide and ensure its proposed Tariff revisions consistently reflect that characterization.  We also encourage PJM to consider providing a description of how it will transition from any proposed types of service back to its traditional market structures and how it will avoid a long-term bifurcation of loads in the PJM market.  Although we are rejecting PJM’s proposal, PJM may consider refiling an alternative proposal under FPA section 205 that considers the guidance provided herein.

ROSNER, Commissioner, concurring: 

I agree with the decision to reject the bulk of PJM’s filing for the reasons articulated in today’s order.  I write separately to emphasize that, if PJM chooses to refile its proposal, it must justify its proposal to curtail IRAS load on a mandatory basis before load that has voluntarily enrolled in a demand response program.  I also urge PJM to carefully consider the consequences any refiled proposal might have on its capacity market.
Customers in a demand response program allow a utility to reduce their demand without resorting to the extreme measure of manually pulling breakers on the utility’s distribution network.  Demand response customers also receive payments in exchange for volunteering to reduce their usage when the grid is stressed.  This structure is designed to protect consumers and their equipment from the draconian measure of being involuntarily forced off the system, as well as to send efficient market signals based on actual system conditions.
PJM’s filing flips this paradigm, proposing to force IRAS load off the system in the earliest stages of emergency conditions, before PJM deploys demand response.  
Moreover, PJM’s proposal would force IRAS load off the system in lieu of sending capacity price signals that are needed to get new infrastructure built.  Because PJM would forcibly curtail IRAS load before other firm load, PJM excludes IRAS load from its capacity market demand curve.  The result could be a capacity market signaling that PJM has more than enough capacity while the region sheds thousands of megawatts of demand on an involuntary basis.  That’s not only economically inefficient, but also likely to prevent supply and demand from coming back into balance.  
To be clear, in an emergency, data centers not serving critical functions should be shut off before ordinary customers (Hint: homes, hospitals, and schools should never be curtailed before data centers).  We need state regulators to establish clear rules for which customers should be curtailed first when circumstances require it.  And we need PJM to be ready to adjust their operations to this evolving paradigm.  But such measures should only be taken when necessary to keep the system reliable, after voluntary demand response resources have been exhausted.  

For these reasons, I respectfully concur.
